newsitem.title: JAPAN: Former star copper trader Hamanaka goes on trial.
newsitem.headline: Former star copper trader Hamanaka goes on trial.

text.p: One-time copper market king Yasuo Hamanaka goes on trial on Monday, charged with defrauding his company with unauthorised trades that created losses of $2.6 billion.

The case, the biggest financial fraud in history, has raised questions of how one person could have amassed such losses without anyone's knowledge and whether Japan properly scrutinises its financial sector.
His employer of 26 years, trading firm Sumitomo Corp, says that Hamanaka acted alone in creating a secret network of trading partners to carry out his improper activities.
He faces up to 15 years in prison for forging documents to open the accounts and for defrauding his company through a "breach of trust".
The trial is expected to offer the first details of how Hamanaka operated.
But it is not likely to shed much light on the broader questions of the extent to which he controlled the world copper market through his extensive holdings.
Rumours have repeatedly surfaced over the past decade that Hamanaka had a virtual lock on the market, driving prices up even as inventories rose.

Sumitomo's chief legal officer said late last year that the company had uncovered no evidence of an attempt to control the market. The company now says that it will not comment on the issue and adds that its internal investigation continues.
"We'd like to finish the investigation as soon as possible, but cannot make comment on when," a Sumitomo spokesman said last week.

Hamanaka has made no public comments since his arrest in October and his lawyers have refused to discuss their defence. His chief lawyer has said previously that his client may admit to the less-serious charge of forging documents.
Unless there is a guilty plea, the trial is expected to be lengthy. Under Japan's legal system, there are often weeks between court sessions in a specific case.
Like the Daiwa Bank scandal before it, the case has raised questions about Japan's financial regulations.
In that case, a bond trader working in Daiwa Bank's New York office was sentenced to four years in prison for hiding losses of $1.1 billion in unauthorised trades.
Japanese authorities say questions of market manipulation are not their problem since the trading took place overseas.
They have left the matter up to U.S. and British regulators who have launched their own probes into the affair.
